facts.text: Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 on an island in the lowest part of a basin with no natural outlet for its water.
Chinampa is the Aztec name for a farming system of plots built in the middle of a lake; the plots are also known as floating gardens.
The growth of Tenochtitlan (today Mexico City) went together with the growth of the chinampa system.
A chinampa is built where the lake has a firm bottom and is only 30 to 60 cm deep.
Stakes of a native willow, the ahuejote, mark the edges of the plot and later grow into trees.
Reeds are woven around the stakes to make a fence that keeps the mud and plant matter from falling into the lake.
The plot is filled with layers of water plants and weeds and then mud from the lake floor, repeated until it rises above the water.
As the plant matter rots, it forms rich soil.
Willow roots hold the edges against erosion and fix the chinampa to the lake bottom.
A chinampa is a rectangle about 20 m long and no more than about 12 m wide, so moisture from the canals can soak into it.
The narrow shape lets farmers water crops and harvest from a canoe.
The canals are about 4 to 6 m wide and serve as transport routes for canoes carrying goods.
Chinampas allow several harvests a year (FAO gives up to five).
After the Spanish conquest in 1521 the city was destroyed and the native water system was largely neglected.
Over the following centuries the lakes around Mexico City were drained to control flooding, and they shrank greatly.
Lake Xochimilco in Mexico City is one of the few places where chinampa farming continues.
Most of today's chinampas grow vegetables and the rest grow flowers.
Chinampa areas are shrinking because Mexico City keeps expanding.
FAO has designated the chinampa system a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System (GIAHS).
